summary: Proposes two changes to the IMP-to-Host protocol to improve communication between users and the network: expanding the Host-Going-Down message and adding a Dead-Host-Status message.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 611 proposes adding expected return times and reason codes to host shutdown information. It also adds a message that lets an IMP report why a destination host is unreachable.

questions: why did arpanet hosts need status codes
what did the dead host status message report
how did a host give its expected return time
subtitle: Changes that let IMP/Host messages explain host shutdowns and outages.

tldr.problem: Existing IMP/Host messages could report that a host was going down or was unreachable, but did not provide enough information about its return time or the reason.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal adds a return-time and reason field to Host-Going-Down messages and introduces a type 6 Dead Host Status message with status information about an unreachable destination.
tldr.outcome: The RFC urges hosts to implement the changes and warns that older hosts may treat the new type 6 message as an error.

today: RFC 611 is a protocol change notice for IMP/Host messages describing host shutdowns and unreachable destinations.

sections.title: Expanded Host-Going-Down Message
sections.content:
The RFC reminds hosts to pass on IMP-Going-Down information to network and local users, and to retain it after the IMP goes down. It then expands the type 2 Host-Going-Down message so a host can state when it expects to return and why it is going down.

Bits 17–28 encode the return day, hour and five-minute interval in Universal Time. A value of all ones means the return is more than a week away; all ones except bit 28 set to zero means the return time is unknown. Bits 29–32 give a reason code, including scheduled maintenance or work, emergency restart, power outage, software breakpoint or hardware failure.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can include when it expects to return and why it is going down. The time uses a day, hour and five-minute interval, and a code gives the reason.

sections.title: Dead Host Status Message
sections.content:
The new type 6 Dead Host Status message lets an IMP send status information about a destination host that is not communicating. It uses bits 17–28 for the same time encoding and bits 29–32 for a status or reason. Codes distinguish unknown cause, a host taking down its ready line without explanation, a host declared down for not taking traffic, a host not known to the NCC, and the stated shutdown reasons.

When the four-bit field is 0, 1, 2 or 3, the time field must indicate unknown. Bit 1 is always zero; a host receiving a type 6 message with bit 1 set to 1 should discard it without reporting an error.
sections.plainLanguage: An IMP can send a separate message explaining why a destination host is unreachable. The message includes a reason code and, when known, the same expected-return time used in a shutdown notice.

sections.title: Delivery and Compatibility
sections.content:
The Dead Host Status message should follow shortly after each Destination Host Dead message. Unlike that message, it is not limited to one message-id or link; users connected to the dead host should be notified of the status information.

The RFC says the changes were to enter the network soon and urges hosts to implement support. It describes the changes as backward compatible except that an older host may receive an unfamiliar type 6 message and log it as an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The new status information applies to all users connected to the unavailable host. Older hosts may not recognize the new message and could log it as an error.
